# Factors and `switch()` to enums and `match` {#sec-enums}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

A factor stores values that come from a fixed set of levels, and `switch()` picks code according to which value it's given. Rust combines both ideas in one feature. An enum is a type whose values come from a fixed list of *variants*, and `match` runs different code for each variant. The compiler knows the full list, so it rejects a value that isn't on it and a `match` that leaves one out. Variants can also carry data, which makes an enum a second way, besides a trait, to represent several kinds of distribution. The matching material in the Rust book is "Enums and Pattern Matching", with more on patterns in "Patterns and Matching" [@rustbook, chaps. 6, 19].

## Factors and enums

A factor records each value as one of its levels:

```{r}
#| label: r-factor
severity <- factor(c("low", "high", "low"),
                   levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
severity
levels(severity)
as.integer(severity)
```

A Rust enum lists its variants, and each value is one of them:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-enum
#[derive(Debug)]
enum Severity {
    Low,
    Medium,
    High,
}

fn main() {
    let readings = vec![Severity::Low, Severity::High, Severity::Low];
    println!("{:?}", readings);
}
```

A variant is written with the enum's name, `Severity::Low`, the same `::` used for `Normal::new()` in @sec-structs. The `#[derive(Debug)]` line works for enums as it does for structs.

The difference shows up with a value that isn't on the list. R turns it into `NA`, without a warning:

```{r}
#| label: r-factor-bad-level
factor("extreme", levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
```

In Rust, `Severity::Extreme` is a compile error, because the enum has no such variant. That check covers names written in the code. Text that arrives while the program runs, such as a column read from a file, has to be converted to a `Severity` first, and the conversion decides what to do with an unknown label, such as returning `None`. Once a value is a `Severity`, though, it's always one of the three variants.

::: {.callout-tip title="The same idea in R"}
An ordered factor, created with `ordered = TRUE`, can be compared with `<` in the order of its levels. Adding `PartialEq` and `PartialOrd` to the `derive` list does the same for an enum like `Severity`, so `Severity::Low < Severity::High` is `true`, in the order the variants are declared. And just as `as.integer()` exposes a factor's codes, `Severity::High as i32` gives the variant's position, counting from zero: `2`. The cast works only for enums whose variants hold no data.
:::

## `switch()` and `match`

In R, `switch()` chooses a value according to a string:

```{r}
#| label: r-switch
weight <- function(level) {
  switch(level, low = 1, medium = 2, high = 4)
}

weight("high")
weight("extreme")
is.null(weight("extreme"))
```

A string with no matching case falls through: `switch()` returns `NULL`, invisibly, so `weight("extreme")` prints nothing at all. The argument has to be a string, too. Given a factor, `switch()` warns and picks a case by the factor's integer code, not by name, so convert a factor's values with `as.character()` first.

Rust's `match` must cover every variant, and leaving one out is a compile error:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-match-missing
#| error: true
enum Severity {
    Low,
    Medium,
    High,
}

fn weight(level: Severity) -> f64 {
    match level {
        Severity::Low => 1.0,
        Severity::Medium => 2.0,
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", weight(Severity::High));
}
```

The error names the variant that isn't handled. Each arm of a `match` has a pattern, `=>`, and the value or block to use when the pattern fits. Like `if` in @sec-setup, a `match` is an expression, so its value is the value of the arm that ran.

When several variants should be handled the same way, `_` matches anything not handled by an earlier arm:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-match-wildcard
# enum Severity {
#     Low,
#     Medium,
#     High,
# }
#
fn weight(level: Severity) -> f64 {
    match level {
        Severity::High => 4.0,
        _ => 1.0,
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", weight(Severity::High));
    println!("{}", weight(Severity::Low));
}
```

This is the same `_` that appeared in `print_type(_: T)` in @sec-types: a pattern that matches anything and ignores it. It's also the counterpart of the unnamed last argument of `switch()`, which supplies a default.

::: {.callout-note title="An R habit to drop in Rust"}
A `switch()` without a default quietly returns `NULL` for anything it doesn't recognize, so careful R code adds a final `stop()`. In Rust, prefer listing every variant over `_`. Then, if someone adds a variant later, every `match` that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error that points to the code needing an update. A `_` arm would silently take the new variant instead.
:::

## Variants with data

A variant can hold values, like a struct. R has nothing built in for this. The closest R code keeps a tag in each object and switches on it:

```{r}
#| label: r-tagged-list
dist_mean <- function(dist) {
  switch(dist$family,
    normal = dist$mean,
    uniform = (dist$min + dist$max) / 2
  )
}
dist_variance <- function(dist) {
  switch(dist$family,
    normal = dist$sd^2,
    uniform = (dist$max - dist$min)^2 / 12
  )
}

normal_dist <- list(family = "normal", mean = 0, sd = 2)
uniform_dist <- list(family = "uniform", min = 0, max = 6)
c(dist_mean(normal_dist), dist_variance(normal_dist))
c(dist_mean(uniform_dist), dist_variance(uniform_dist))
is.null(dist_mean(list(family = "exponential", rate = 2)))
```

Here's the running class as an enum, named `Dist` to keep it apart from the `Distribution` trait:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-enum-data
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum Dist {
    Normal { mean: f64, sd: f64 },
    Uniform { min: f64, max: f64 },
}

fn mean(dist: Dist) -> f64 {
    match dist {
        Dist::Normal { mean, .. } => mean,
        Dist::Uniform { min, max } => (min + max) / 2.0,
    }
}

fn variance(dist: Dist) -> f64 {
    match dist {
        Dist::Normal { sd, .. } => sd * sd,
        Dist::Uniform { min, max } => (max - min).powi(2) / 12.0,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let dists = vec![
        Dist::Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 2.0 },
        Dist::Uniform { min: 0.0, max: 6.0 },
    ];
    for dist in dists {
        println!(
            "{:?}: mean {}, variance {}",
            dist,
            mean(dist),
            variance(dist)
        );
    }
}
```

A pattern such as `Dist::Normal { mean, .. }` matches a `Normal` and names its `mean` field for use in the arm; `..` ignores the rest. Because `Dist` is a single type, a plain `Vec<Dist>` holds both kinds of distribution, with no `Box` or `dyn` (@sec-generics). Deriving `Clone` and `Copy` lets `dist` be passed to both functions, as in @sec-operators.

An enum is the R pattern with the tags checked. Add an `Exponential` variant to `Dist`, and both `mean()` and `variance()` stop compiling until they handle it. Add an `"exponential"` family in R, and `dist_mean()` returns `NULL` for it, as the last line of the R code shows.

## Enums or traits

The running class now exists in two forms: as types that implement the `Distribution` trait (@sec-s3-traits) and as variants of the `Dist` enum. The two forms differ in what a change costs:

| | Trait with one type per distribution | Enum with one variant per distribution |
|----------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Adding a distribution | Write a new type and its `impl`, anywhere, even in another crate | Add a variant, then update every `match` without a `_` arm |
| Adding an operation | Add a method to the trait, then update every `impl`, unless the method has a default | Write one new function with a `match` |
| The set of distributions | Open | Closed, listed in one place |
| A collection of mixed distributions | `Vec<Box<dyn Distribution>>` | `Vec<Dist>` |
| Closest R equivalent | S3 or S4 classes with methods | A `switch()` on a tag, or an S4 class union |

An operation that needs only the trait's existing methods can also be a plain function, like `sum_moments()` in @sec-multiple-dispatch, with no change to the trait.

S4's `setClassUnion()`, mentioned in @sec-s4, sits on the enum side: it gathers the classes that count as one into a single list. Unlike an enum's variants, that list can grow later.

## `Option` is an enum

@sec-missingness used `Option` with `if let` and `unwrap_or()`. It's an ordinary enum from the standard library, with two variants: `Some`, which holds a value, and `None`. Unlike `Severity`'s variants, they need no prefix, because Rust makes them available in every program [@rustbook, sec. 6.1]. A `match` handles both cases directly:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-match-option
let reading: Option<f64> = None;
let text = match reading {
    Some(value) => format!("reading: {value}"),
    None => String::from("no reading"),
};
println!("{text}");
```

In Rust, `if let` is shorthand for a `match` with one pattern: its block runs when the pattern matches, and an `else` block, if there is one, handles everything else. The `Result` type from @sec-s4 is an enum as well, with variants `Ok` and `Err`.

## Matching on pairs

@sec-multiple-dispatch promised a workaround for choosing code from the runtime types of two values. With an enum, `match` can take a pair of values, written `(a, b)`, and give an arm to each combination:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-match-pair
# #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
# enum Dist {
#     Normal { mean: f64, sd: f64 },
#     Uniform { min: f64, max: f64 },
# }
#
fn add(a: Dist, b: Dist) -> Option<Dist> {
    match (a, b) {
        (
            Dist::Normal { mean: m1, sd: s1 },
            Dist::Normal { mean: m2, sd: s2 },
        ) => Some(Dist::Normal {
            mean: m1 + m2,
            sd: (s1 * s1 + s2 * s2).sqrt(),
        }),
        _ => None,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let n = Dist::Normal { mean: 0.0, sd: 3.0 };
    let u = Dist::Uniform { min: 0.0, max: 6.0 };
    println!("{:?}", add(n, Dist::Normal { mean: 1.0, sd: 4.0 }));
    println!("{:?}", add(n, u));
}
```

The parentheses make a *tuple*, a fixed group of values that can have different types, and a tuple's type is written the same way, here `(Dist, Dist)` [@rustbook, sec. 3.2]. The patterns name the fields of both values: `mean: m1` binds the first normal's mean to `m1`. Every other pair falls to `_` and returns `None`, because their sum isn't one of the distributions in `Dist`. The choice is made at runtime, from the values themselves, so this works for elements of a `Vec<Dist>` whose kinds aren't known in advance, which is what S4's multiple dispatch does with classes.

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `factor(x, levels = ...)` | `enum Severity { Low, Medium, High }` |
| An unknown level becomes `NA` | An unknown variant doesn't compile |
| `ordered = TRUE` | `#[derive(PartialEq, PartialOrd)]` |
| `as.integer(f)` | `Severity::High as i32` |
| Without a default, `switch()` returns `NULL` when nothing matches | `match` must cover every variant |
| The unnamed default of `switch()` | `_ =>` |
| A list with a `family` tag | An enum variant with fields |
| `setClassUnion()`, which can gain members later | An enum, whose variants are fixed |
| Multiple dispatch on runtime classes | `match` on a pair of enum values |
